evidence.claim: South of New Castle, Route 9 runs through rural Delaware as a two-lane road west of the river and bay.
evidence.quote: DE 9 is a designated scenic highway known as the Delaware Bayshore Byway south of New Castle, running through mostly rural areas to the west of the Delaware Bay and the Delaware River as a two-lane undivided road.

evidence.claim: DelDOT highlights coastal marshlands, wildlife, farming heritage and historic river towns along the Delaware Bayshore Byway, designated a National Scenic Byway in 2021.
evidence.quote: In 2021, the Delaware Bayshore Byway received designation from the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Federal Highway Administration as a National Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: highlights coastal marshlands, wildlife, farming heritage and historic river towns along the Delaware Bayshore Byway, designated a National Scenic Byway in 2021.
evidence.quote: The byway corridor features 19 Discovery Zones which offers visitors and locals an intimate experience featuring coastal marshlands, abundant wildlife, rich hunting, fishing, and farming heritage and historic river and bay towns and communities.

evidence.claim: The older Route 9 Coastal Heritage corridor is now part of that longer journey, which continues south toward Lewes.
evidence.quote: The Delaware Bayshore Byway (formerly Route 9 Coastal Heritage Byway) runs along the Delaware Bay and Delaware River from Lewes north to New Castle, with the southern portion consisting of several roads providing access to the Delaware Bay and the northern portion following DE 9;

evidence.claim: The corridor lies within the Atlantic Flyway, where migrating shorebirds feed and rest each spring before continuing to northern breeding grounds.
evidence.quote: The byway lies entirely within the Atlantic Flyway where each spring, hundreds of thousands of migrating shorebirds can be found feeding and resting while they continue their journey to their northern breeding grounds.

evidence.claim: The campaign began well before the new name: the state highway department recommended scenic status for Route 9 in 1965.
evidence.quote: As far back as 1965, Delaware State Highway Department recommended that State Route 9 be designated a scenic highway.

evidence.claim: Residents, public officials, nonprofit groups and agencies joined to nominate it in 2003; state designation followed in 2007.
evidence.quote: In 2003 a broad coalition of Rt 9 residents, State and local politicians, not-for-profit organizations and State and local agencies came together to nominate Route 9 as a State Scenic Byway. On March 7, 2007, Rt9 was designated a DE Scenic and Historic Byway.

evidence.claim: The byway took the Delaware Bayshore name in 2013, and DelDOT accepted its southern extension in 2017.
evidence.quote: 2013: Byway was officially renamed the Delaware Bayshore Byway

evidence.claim: DelDOT accepted its southern extension in 2017.
evidence.quote: 2017: Southern Extension of Byway officially accepted by DelDOT

evidence.claim: The courthouse cupola gives New Castle a place in the geometry of state borders: it is the center of the Twelve-Mile Circle defining much of Delaware’s boundary with Pennsylvania.
evidence.quote: The cupola of the court house is the center of the "Twelve-Mile Circle" that defines much of the border between Delaware and Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: The building was Delaware’s colonial capitol and first State House, and served as a courthouse until 1882.
evidence.quote: New Castle Court House Museum, the original colonial capitol and first State House of Delaware, served as the courthouse until 1882,

evidence.claim: Government moved south to Dover in 1777; the county seat later moved to Wilmington.
evidence.quote: the government elected to move its functions south to Dover in May, 1777.

evidence.claim: The town’s central green dates to the Dutch street plan.
evidence.quote: Dutch authorities laid out a grid of streets and established a common green in the town's center, which continues to this day.

evidence.claim: Route 9 itself bypasses the historic area on its passage through New Castle.
evidence.quote: Delaware Route 9 runs southwest-to-northeast through New Castle, passing through the city along 7th Street, Washington Street, Delaware Street, and Ferry Cut Off Street; the route bypasses the historic area.

evidence.claim: Before it became Odessa, the port was called Cantwell’s Bridge.
evidence.quote: Odessa was originally known as Cantwell's Bridge. In 1721, a son of Captain Edmund Cantwell opened a toll bridge over the Appoquinimink Creek at this location.

evidence.claim: In 1721, a son of Captain Edmund Cantwell opened a toll bridge across the creek here.
evidence.quote: In 1721, a son of Captain Edmund Cantwell opened a toll bridge over the Appoquinimink Creek at this location.

evidence.claim: The port shipped wheat, corn, tobacco and produce down Appoquinimink Creek to Delaware Bay and distant ports.
evidence.quote: Cantwell's Bridge became an important port that shipped wheat, corn, tobacco, and produce down the creek to the Delaware Bay, where it traveled to distant ports.

evidence.claim: When a railroad was proposed through town, merchants and vessel owners opposed it.
evidence.quote: The railroad was originally proposed to be built through Cantwell's Bridge but the merchants and vessel owners in the town opposed.

evidence.claim: The line went through Middletown instead, and the grain trade collapsed in 1855.
evidence.quote: In 1855, the grain trade collapsed after the Delaware Railroad was built to the west through Middletown.

evidence.claim: Renaming the town Odessa, after the port in the Russian Empire, now Ukraine, was an effort to preserve its commercial future.
evidence.quote: the town was renamed to Odessa after the port city of Odessa in the Russian Empire (present-day Ukraine) in an effort to keep the town alive as a major port.

evidence.claim: A significant part of Odessa is now a historic district.
evidence.quote: Today a significant part of the town is a historic district list on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: Bombay Hook’s tidal marshes share the refuge with freshwater pools shaped by human work.
evidence.quote: They cleared wooded swamps and built a dike to create Raymond and Shearness Pools and a causeway to separate Shearness and Finis Pools, creating three freshwater impoundments;

evidence.claim: Established in 1937 for migratory and wintering waterfowl, the refuge was purchased with federal duck stamp funds.
evidence.quote: It was established on March 16, 1937, as a refuge and breeding ground for migratory and wintering waterfowl along the Atlantic Flyway. The Refuge was purchased from local land owners with federal duck stamp funds.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps crews began work the following year, building a dike and a causeway to create three freshwater impoundments.
evidence.quote: On April 1, 1938, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) based at Leipsic, Delaware started work on the refuge.

evidence.claim: building a dike and a causeway to create three freshwater impoundments.
evidence.quote: They cleared wooded swamps and built a dike to create Raymond and Shearness Pools and a causeway to separate Shearness and Finis Pools, creating three freshwater impoundments;

evidence.claim: Water levels in the pools are managed to encourage plants for waterfowl; drawing them down exposes mudflats where shorebirds and wading birds feed.
evidence.quote: The water levels in the refuge's impoundments are manipulated to produce desirable emergent and underwater plants for waterfowl. When the pools are drawn down, large populations of shore and wading birds feed on the mudflats.

evidence.claim: The salt marsh, intersected by tidal streams and rivers, also serves as a nursery for marine organisms.
evidence.quote: The marsh, with its intersecting tidal streams and rivers, provides excellent natural habitat for birds and mammals and serves as a nursery for marine organisms,
